clue.text: Chief trimmed fish to get by

indicators.note: something trimmed has had its end cut off, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: BEST (chief, top) without its final letter
the ide is a freshwater fish, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A head chef trims a fish just to scrape by.
explanation.definitionFit: Beside and by are both prepositions of position, meaning next to, as in 'sit by me'.

clue.text: Remixed version of Let It Be includes line that's rubbish

indicators.note: a remix rearranges a recording, so the song title's letters are rearranged too

blocks.note: the Beatles song title, taken as letters
L is the usual abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a remix of the Beatles' Let It Be as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' looks like a noun at the end of the critic's verdict, but it is the verb, to rubbish someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish someone is to disparage or run them down, which is exactly what belittling does.

clue.text: Military leaders for the most part filmed with weapons

indicators.note: only most of the word is wanted, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: SHOT (filmed) without its last letter
guns are weapons

explanation.surface: Generals were mostly filmed carrying weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoguns were the hereditary military commanders who effectively ruled feudal Japan.

clue.text: Put an end to role of senior policeman?

blocks.note: a DI is a detective inspector; 'of' makes it possessive, DI'S
to take on someone's mantle is to assume their role

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a senior officer's job is to be abolished.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks about scrapping a job, but the clue is read as a possessive phrase: a detective inspector's cloak of office, run together as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle a scheme or organisation is to take it apart and so bring it to an end.

clue.text: Placing rest behind ball on table leads to slight stretch

indicators.note: putting one thing behind another sets it second, so the resting word follows the snooker term

blocks.note: the white is the cue ball on a snooker or pool table
to lie is to rest; 'placing behind' puts it after the ball

explanation.surface: A snooker player places the rest behind the cue ball, stretching across the table.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker the rest is a cue support, which makes 'rest' look like equipment rather than the verb to lie.
explanation.definitionFit: A white lie is a small harmless untruth, a minor stretching of the truth.

clue.text: Cool music genre causes mirth, entertaining half of retiring Tory big beasts

indicators.note: only half the word is kept, the first two of its four letters
to retire is to go back, so the kept letters are read backwards
to entertain is to host, so one piece takes the other inside it

blocks.note: hip means fashionable, cool
pop music
to amuse is to cause laughter
the first half of the word

explanation.surface: A cool music genre amuses people by mocking big beasts of the retiring Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big beasts' is the political phrase for heavyweight politicians, which suits the Tory surface, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippopotamuses are among the largest land animals, so they are literally big beasts.

clue.text: This person seen putting down beer regularly in alcohol-free region

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken, starting from the first
the letters sit inside the abbreviation for teetotal

blocks.note: TT is short for teetotal, drinking no alcohol
the setter refers to themselves
first and third letters

explanation.surface: Someone is seen giving up beer regularly while in a region where alcohol is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting down' means writing: the I is written down followed by the selected letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tibet is an autonomous region of China on the Himalayan plateau.

clue.text: "Noisy thing" tucking into nut roast

indicators.note: something tucking into another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a nut and a loon are both crazy people
an amp (amplifier) makes things loud

explanation.surface: A noisy diner tucks into a nut roast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut roast' is a vegetarian dish, but here 'nut' is a person and 'roast' is the verb to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast someone is to ridicule them mercilessly, which is what a lampoon does to its target.

clue.text: Seven sonnets edited down becoming all the same

indicators.note: cut back at both ends, the phrase keeps only an inner run of letters

blocks.note: the inner letters of the two words, ends cut away

explanation.surface: Seven sonnets were cut down until they all sounded alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Even so and all the same are both phrases meaning nevertheless, conceding a point.

clue.text: Martial artist praises this liquefied food

indicators.note: melted into liquid, the words lose their shape and reform

blocks.note: a dan is a black-belt grade, and a holder of one, in judo and karate
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A martial artist praises a liquid diet.
explanation.definitionFit: Danish pastries are sweet flaky baked goods, a kind of food.

clue.text: Glimpse small instrument and step on it

blocks.note: a glimpse is a quick look
S for small, as on clothing labels
the harp is a musical instrument

explanation.surface: Someone spots a small instrument on the floor and treads on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step on it' reads as literally treading on the instrument, but it is the idiom for hurry up.
explanation.definitionFit: Look sharp and step on it are both commands telling someone to hurry.

clue.text: Case for bistro to be presented with award for dessert

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters
an MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A bistro receives an award for its dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombe is a frozen dome-shaped pudding, usually of ice cream, served as a dessert.

clue.text: High roller?

blocks.note: surface reading: a big gambler who stakes large sums
setter's reading: a very tall wave that rolls in from the sea

explanation.walkthrough: A high roller is a big-spending gambler; a roller is also a long heavy wave, and the highest waves of all come from undersea earthquakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a huge sea wave, and a roller is a crossword-friendly word for a large breaking wave.

clue.text: Tops made from animals on sale first

blocks.note: a product that is out has been released and is available; 'first' puts it at the front
does are female deer

explanation.surface: Clothing tops made from animal skins go on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tops' looks like a noun for garments, but it is the verb meaning beats.
explanation.definitionFit: To top someone is to better them, and outdoes means surpasses in the same way.

clue.text: Composer's pitch to those in the Albert Hall?

indicators.text: to those in the Albert Hall
indicators.note: a concert audience hears rather than reads, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a ship that pitches or leans over lists

explanation.surface: A composer pitches his work to a concert audience at the Albert Hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Albert Hall is a major London concert venue. 'Pitch' looks musical, but it is a lean.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the nineteenth-century Hungarian composer and piano virtuoso.

clue.text: Trick shot at Lord's inspiring Derbyshire's opening victory

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece is taken inside another
the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the hook is a cricket stroke; Lord's is London's famous cricket ground
first letter
a victory is a win

explanation.surface: A trick shot at Lord's helps Derbyshire, a county cricket side, to open with a victory.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoodwink someone is to deceive them, to trick them.

clue.text: Car-sick, we abandoned Sally

indicators.note: abandoned in the sense of wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Feeling car-sick, the travellers left their friend Sally behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally looks like a woman's name, but a sally is a witty retort.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a quick witty remark, so it is a synonym of a wisecrack.

clue.text: Judges order them from the Bar?

blocks.note: first meaning: assesses or gauges, a verb
second meaning: what drinkers ask for at the pub bar, set quantities of spirits

explanation.walkthrough: Judges and the Bar make it sound like the legal profession; the Bar here is a pub counter.
explanation.definitionFit: To measure something is to evaluate it, and pub drinks are served in standard quantities of spirit.

clue.text: Sweetener given back: ultra-rare medal more than suffices

indicators.note: the phrase holds more letters than needed, so the word sits inside it
something given back is returned, so the letters are read in the other direction

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A sporting hero hands back an ultra-rare medal, a sweet gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara is a light brown cane sugar, used to sweeten coffee.

clue.text: Surfaces of puzzle finally come together with tip from subeditor

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the word
the tip of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: last letter
to merge is to come together
first letter

explanation.surface: A subeditor's tip brings the surfaces of a puzzle together at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surfaces' reads as a noun, but it is the verb, comes up into view.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that surfaces emerges, coming up into the open from below.

clue.text: Woman is about to enter appeal

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the short word is read backwards
one piece enters, going inside the other

blocks.note: to sue is to appeal to a court
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman is about to launch an appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie is a woman's given name, short for Susan.

clue.text: Rod Stewart's first big house occupied by Neil Diamond initially

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the singer's surname
initially takes the first letter of each of the two names
a house occupied by people has them inside it

blocks.note: first letter
a pile is a large stately house
the initials

explanation.surface: Rod Stewart's first mansion was occupied by fellow singer Neil Diamond.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod sits at the front like the singer's first name, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A spindle is a slender rod on which thread is wound or something turns.

clue.text: Imagine writer's notes being nicked by flipping Gallagher?

indicators.note: a thing flipped is turned over, so the name is read backwards
something nicked is taken and held, so one piece ends up inside the other

blocks.note: Noel Gallagher, songwriter of the band Oasis
nn. is the abbreviation for notes

explanation.surface: Noel Gallagher, a flipping Lennon fan, steals the songwriter's notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imagine' looks like an invitation, but it is the song title.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lennon wrote and recorded the song Imagine in 1971.

clue.text: Perhaps Iron Maiden given small space on set with time moved to the end

indicators.note: a letter is shifted from the front to the back of the word

blocks.note: TELE, a television set, with its T for time taken off the front
M is a maiden over in cricket scoring
an en is a small printer's space, half an em
T for time, now placed last

explanation.surface: The heavy metal band Iron Maiden get a small spot on a TV set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Maiden' reads as the rock band; split apart, 'Perhaps Iron' is the definition and Maiden starts the wordplay. The T of the set moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron is a chemical element, so it is an example of one, signalled by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Hoovered each mid-morning

blocks.note: ea. is the abbreviation for each
ten o'clock is the middle of the morning

explanation.surface: Someone vacuumed every day in the middle of the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: To hoover is to vacuum-clean (Hoover being a British vacuum brand), but it is also slang for eating greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoover up food is to wolf it down, so hoovered food has been eaten.

clue.text: Repellent game features unpleasant juveniles

indicators.note: to repel is to drive back, so the letters are pushed into reverse

blocks.note: RU is rugby union
chins are facial features

explanation.surface: A disgusting game is full of nasty youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repellent' looks like an adjective for the game, but it signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Urchins are mischievous, often scruffy children, so unpleasant youngsters.

clue.text: Republican abandoning his political position, say, for new dark period

indicators.note: one letter leaves its place and another is put in for it

blocks.note: a Republican's place on the political spectrum is the right
R for Republican, the letter that goes
N for new, the letter that comes in

explanation.surface: A Republican abandons his political stance and heads into a dark new era.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the time of darkness between sunset and sunrise.

clue.text: European drink Dharma promoted capturing style

indicators.note: promoted means moved up, so one letter goes to the front
something capturing another holds it inside

blocks.note: CIDER, with the I that stands for the setter Dharma moved up to the front
elan is flair, style

explanation.surface: A European promotes a drink called Dharma that has real style.
explanation.walkthrough: The I in the drink stands for the setter; promoting it moves it to the front before the style is captured.
explanation.definitionFit: An Icelander is a native of Iceland, a European country.

clue.text: Ultimately Lloyds or Barclays bound by primary point – to give extra interest

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter, which both bank names share
something bound by another is enclosed within it

blocks.note: No. 1, number one, with the 1 as I
the last letter of either
a ness is a headland, a point of land

explanation.surface: High-street banks Lloyds and Barclays offer bonus interest at a key point.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyds and Barclays are British banks, which makes 'interest' look financial.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosiness is an excessive curiosity in other people's affairs, more interest than is welcome.

clue.text: Those not wanting Labour to lose heart, they're on a slippery slope

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, which is removed

blocks.note: skivers dodge work; 'labour' here is just work

explanation.surface: Voters deserting the Labour party lose heart as it heads down a slippery slope.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour suggests the British political party, but it is plain work. A skiver is British slang for a shirker.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiers glide down snowy slopes, literally on a slippery slope, rather than in the idiom's sense.
